title: Implantation and pregnancy
focus: From one cell to a growing baby
notes: The baby develops in the uterus.
Embryo and fetus are stages of development.
Follow the organs, cells and timeline.
narration: Welcome to CBE STEM Academy, Grade Seven Integrated Science. How does a fertilised egg become a baby?
We will follow early cell division, implantation, and growth inside the uterus. Watch the labels and follow each stage.

title: The journey to the uterus
focus: A dividing ball of cells travels along the tube
notes: Zygote means fertilised egg.
One cell divides into two, then four.
Tiny hairs and tube movements help transport.
narration: Fertilisation usually happens in a fallopian tube. The new single cell is called a zygote. It divides into two cells, then four, and then many more.
The group of cells moves towards the uterus. Tiny hairs and movements of the tube help carry it. The cells do not swim like sperm.

title: A blastocyst forms
focus: A hollow ball of cells gets ready to attach
notes: Outer cells help form the placenta.
Inner cells develop into the embryo.
The protective outer coat is shed.
narration: After several days, a hollow ball of cells forms. This stage is called a blastocyst. Look for its outer cells, fluid-filled space, and small group of inner cells.
The inner cells will develop into the embryo. The blastocyst comes out of its protective coat before attaching to the uterus.

title: Implantation: attaching to the lining
focus: Attachment begins about 6–7 days after fertilisation
notes: The lining is called the endometrium.
Outer cells attach, then embed in the lining.
Implantation takes place over several days.
narration: The uterus has a soft, blood-rich inner lining called the endometrium. About six to seven days after fertilisation, the blastocyst begins to attach to this lining.
Its outer cells help it settle into the lining. This gradual process is called implantation. It is not a baby sticking to the outside of the uterus.
The lining supports early development. Implantation takes several days. The tiny developing embryo stays inside the uterus, where it can continue to grow.

title: The embryo begins to take shape
focus: Cells become different tissues and organs
notes: The brain and spinal cord begin forming.
The heart and limb buds develop.
Organs continue to grow and mature.
narration: After implantation, cells grow and take on different jobs. Some help form the brain and spinal cord. Others form the heart, muscles, and other body parts.
Small arm and leg buds appear. The developing human is called an embryo during these early weeks. The organs are beginning to form; they are not fully mature.

title: Placenta and umbilical cord
focus: A connection for oxygen, nutrients and wastes
notes: Placenta: attached to the uterine wall.
Cord: connects placenta to the baby's abdomen.
The two blood supplies normally stay separate.
narration: A temporary organ called the placenta develops where the pregnancy attaches to the uterine lining. An umbilical cord connects the developing baby to the placenta.
Oxygen and nutrients pass from the mother's blood across the placenta to the baby's blood. Carbon dioxide and other wastes pass back in the other direction.
The two blood supplies normally stay separate. The cord carries blood between the baby and placenta. The baby does not eat through its mouth inside the uterus.

title: A protected place to grow
focus: Amniotic sac, fluid and muscular uterus
notes: The amniotic sac surrounds the baby.
Amniotic fluid cushions movement.
The cervix is the lower opening of the uterus.
narration: The baby is surrounded by a thin bag called the amniotic sac. Inside it, amniotic fluid cushions the baby and allows movement.
The uterus has strong muscular walls. Its lower opening is the cervix. During most of pregnancy, the cervix stays closed. The baby grows inside the uterus, not inside the stomach.

title: First trimester: the body plan forms
notes: The major body structures begin to form.
Fingers, toes and facial features develop.
Embryo → fetus: a change in stage name.
narration: Pregnancy is divided into three parts called trimesters. During the first trimester, the main body structures begin to form. Arms and legs grow, and fingers and toes develop.
After about eight weeks from fertilisation, the developing baby is called a fetus. That is about ten weeks on the pregnancy calendar. Its organs still need time to mature.

title: Second trimester: growth and movement
notes: Bones and muscles develop further.
The fetus moves its arms and legs.
The uterus expands as the fetus grows.
narration: During the second trimester, the fetus grows larger. Bones and muscles develop further. The arms and legs can move, and the mother may begin to feel movements.
The placenta and cord keep supplying oxygen and nutrients. The uterus expands to make room. The fetus is becoming more developed, but it is not yet ready for birth.

title: Third trimester: preparing for birth
notes: The fetus gains weight and stores fat.
The brain and lungs continue maturing.
Many babies turn head-down before birth.
narration: During the third trimester, the fetus gains weight and stores fat. The brain and lungs continue to mature. There is less space as the baby grows, but movement continues.
Many babies turn so their head points towards the cervix before birth. Look at the placenta on the uterine wall and the cord leading to the baby's abdomen.
This model speeds up months of growth. Real development happens gradually, and the timing varies between pregnancies.

title: Gestation: how long does pregnancy last?
focus: About 40 pregnancy weeks; about 38 after fertilisation
notes: Gestation is the period of development before birth.
Pregnancy weeks start from the last period.
A due date is an estimate, not an exact promise.
narration: The time a baby develops in the uterus before birth is called gestation. Human pregnancy usually lasts about forty weeks, or roughly nine months, counted from the first day of the last menstrual period.
That is about thirty-eight weeks after fertilisation. These are two ways of counting the same pregnancy. Birth does not always happen on the estimated due date.

title: Pause, remember and explain
notes: Where does implantation happen?
What do the placenta and cord do?
How long is human gestation?
narration: Pause and answer. Where does implantation happen? What do the placenta and cord do? How long is human gestation?
Check: implantation happens in the uterine lining. The placenta and cord support exchange with the baby. Pregnancy is usually counted as about forty weeks.
